author: Heilprin source tradition; Warsaw digital witness

paragraphs: (1) He was head of the academy for eighty years, like Joseph in Egypt; see part 1, year 3990 [digital witness נ״א, apparently for ג״א]. He would sit at the entrances to immersion so as to answer amen to the blessing over the women’s immersion, and also so that they would picture his beauty and bear children like him (Shalshelet HaKabbalah). He said: ‘I come from Joseph’s seed, over whom the evil eye has no power’: Berakhot 20a and Bava Metzia 84a. He was precise in saying ‘from Joseph’s seed,’ rather than ‘I come from Joseph,’ as Rabbi is said to come from David. Zohar, Bereshit, at the locator ע׳ קנ״ט, says that ten sparks of seed issued from Joseph. He was fit to father twelve tribes like Jacob, in the mystery of ‘These are Jacob’s generations: Joseph’; because ten drops issued from his ten fingernails, he fathered only two. Therefore there were ten martyrs of the government; see there. Yalkut, beginning of Mishlei, says the ten martyrs were on account of the sin of selling Joseph. Galante and Emek HaMelekh say the ten martyrs were not killed: just as the tribes’ intention was not carried out, for Joseph was restored, so it was with the ten martyrs, as I explained at length in my large work; see the ten martyrs. Joseph, through slandering his brothers, caused them to sell him and emitted ten drops; therefore Rabbi Yochanan’s ten sons died. This is the mystery of ‘from Joseph’s seed.’ It is a hint; if I have erred, may the good Lord atone. He was very beautiful, but lacked the glory of the face, meaning a beard, as related in Bava Metzia, HaSokher, 84a. Perhaps this was because Joseph used to curl his hair and emerged without a full beard. He had no armpit hair; Nazir 59a says it had fallen out because of old age. Vayakhel Moshe 46b writes that Rabbi Yochanan was of the feminine aspect, and therefore had no beard; see its explanation there. His eyelids covered his eyes, and he would lift them with a silver fork; see Rashi, Taanit 9a.

(2) Ten of his sons died, for he told Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat: ‘This is a bone of the tenth son.’ They say it was a bone smaller than a barleycorn; some say it was a tooth, which does not convey impurity (Rashbam, Bava Batra 116a; Arukh, entry gerem). Some say ‘the tenth bir’ means a recovery meal, and it was not a human bone. Yuchasin writes in a gloss that he found in Megillat Setarim of Mar Nissan Gaon: nine sons died, and the tenth fell into a boiling cauldron; his flesh melted, and only the bones remained. He took a bone from the little finger and used it to console people. A son remained, named Mattanah, and he immediately sent him to Babylonia to learn with Shmuel; he was Rav Yehudah’s colleague. End quotation. But Bava Batra 116a appears to show that he left no son; see Rashbam there. He had daughters, for he wanted Zeiri to take his daughter; see Zeiri’s entry.

(3) He was called Bar Nappacha. In Chelek 96a Resh Lakish said: ‘The smith’s interpretation is better’—Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha—‘than the smith’s son’s’—Rabbi Yochanan. Rashi explains: throughout the Talmud he is called Bar Nappacha—‘Who will let the smith’s son in?’—because his father was a smith. Another explanation is on account of his beauty, or on account of סגי נהור [provisionally his blindness]. See Chiddushei Aggadot, Bava Metzia 85b, for another reason he was called Bar Nappacha. It requires examination: perhaps his father’s name was Nappacha. Beer Sheva writes: ‘I find it difficult: why did he not call him respectfully “Rabbi,” since he was his principal teacher?’ In Ketubbot 25b Resh Lakish was angry with Rabbi Elazar for not speaking in Rabbi Yochanan’s name, and told him: ‘You heard the smith’s son’s words and did not say them in his name.’ In the Jerusalem Talmud, Rosh Hashanah 2:6, Rabbi Yonatan said concerning Rabbi Yochanan: ‘See the language the smith’s son taught me.’ Yuchasin, in the sequence of amoraim under Rav Ashi, writes: ‘I do not know who his father was.’ In the Jerusalem Talmud, the chapter Af Al Pi, halakhah 6, he recognized the women who had assisted his mother. That is, he did not know his mother, because she died when she bore him, as in Kiddushin 31b: ‘Happy is one who did not see them, such as I: when his mother conceived him, his father died; when he was born, his mother died.’

(4) See Bava Kamma, final chapter, 117, for the great matter that happened between him and his student Rav Kahana. He was not a priest, but merely ate ordinary food in purity; see Yuchasin, sequence of generations under Rabbi Tzadok. The Nasi’s household helped support him, as in Sotah 21a: ‘Not like Yochanan of the Nasi’s house.’ He went into commerce with his colleague Ilfa and heard a voice that the time was favorable for one of them. He heard it and Ilfa did not. He said: ‘We may infer that the time is favorable for me.’ He returned home and was appointed head of the academy; see his entry. He did not wear head tefillin in winter because it harmed him: Jerusalem Talmud, the chapter Hayah Kore, mishnah 3. From this it appears as the Rosh writes in a responsum, general rule 3, part 4, that nothing should intervene beneath either head or arm tefillin. Were it permitted, why would Rabbi Yochanan have omitted the commandment of tefillin instead of putting them on a hat or something else? Rashba too was uncertain and did not permit it, unlike Ran and Bar Sheshet, who permitted it because they had not seen the Jerusalem Talmud. See Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim, section 27. Beit Yosef there cites this Jerusalem Talmud and explains why Rabbi Yochanan did not place them upon his hat. Yuchasin needlessly objected to those permitting it as though they had not seen the Jerusalem Talmud. Beer Sheva 92a writes: in Almanah Nizonet, all work a slave does for his master a student does, except untying a shoe when he has no tefillin on his head, lest people say he is a slave. Untying a shoe is not exclusive: the same applies to other work characteristic of a slave, such as carrying his belongings after him to the bathhouse, acts by which a slave is acquired, as in Kiddushin, chapter 1. Therefore Rabbi Yochanan says in HaMafkid, BaKol Mearvin, and elsewhere: ‘Whoever explains to me,’ and so forth, ‘I shall carry his belongings after him to the bathhouse.’ Because he had no tefillin on his head, he meant: not only shall I honor him as a student honors his teacher, but I shall even do what a student is not obliged to do for his teacher. End quotation. He recited the Shema leaning—that is, lying on his side—because he was corpulent: Berakhot 13b. ‘Rabbi Yochanan was supported by Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi’: some explain that he was hosted by him; others explain that he was corpulent. Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot, beginning of chapter 2, and Moed Katan 3:7. In Shekalim 2:6 the reading is Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba. In Pesikta, quoted in Yalkut at the end of Mishpatim, Rabbi Yochanan walked up from Tiberias to Sepphoris, leaning upon Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba’s shoulder. They reached a field. He said: ‘This was mine, and I sold it because I wished to occupy myself with Torah,’ and so forth. Likewise an olive grove, and likewise a vineyard. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba began to weep, and so forth. He told him: ‘Chiyya, my son, is it a small thing in your eyes that I sold something given in six days—for the world was created in six days—and acquired something given in forty days?’ When he died they applied to him: ‘If a man gave all his house’s wealth for the love with which Rabbi Yochanan loved Torah, they would utterly scorn him.’ Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish said: ‘We merited Torah only because we saw Rabbi’s fingers from his sleeves’: Jerusalem Talmud, end of Mashilin, halakhah 2. In Yevamot 96b Rabbi Yochanan was angry with Rabbi Elazar because he did not speak in his name, and Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi appeased him; see his entry, and the Jerusalem Talmud passages in Berakhot, Shekalim, and Moed Katan cited above. Rabbi Elazar said: ‘I saw Rabbi Yochanan in a dream; I shall say something excellent’; see his entry. Rabbi Yochanan went up a stair; Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi supported him. The stair gave way; he went up and lifted them up: Af Al Pi, 62a. An incident came before him in the synagogue of Maon: Bava Kamma 99b. Rabbi Yochanan went up to Rabbi Yehudah Nesia, who came out to him in a linen garment. Rabbi Yochanan told him: ‘Put on your wool garment, because “Your eyes shall behold a king in his beauty”’: Jerusalem Talmud, end of Kohen Gadol. When he went to greet Rabbi Chanina, he would clear his throat so as not to enter suddenly: Rabbah, Acharei, section 21. Rabbi Yochanan wrote to Shmuel: ‘To our colleague,’ but afterwards said of him: ‘I have a teacher in Babylonia,’ for Rabbi Yochanan was in the Land of Israel; see his entry. They told him Rav had died. He tore thirteen garments for him and said: ‘The man I feared has gone.’ When Rabbi Chanina died, he tore for him, and so forth, saying: ‘Gone,’ and so forth: Moed Katan 24a. Once ravenous hunger seized him, and he ran to the east side of a fig tree: Yoma 83b. Of every food he ate, he gave some to his slave: Jerusalem Talmud, Af Al Pi and HaChovel, halakhah 5. He suffered from tzafidna; a matron taught him a remedy. He swore to her, ‘To the God of Heaven I shall not reveal it,’ and disclosed to her that he would reveal it so that there should be no desecration of God’s name when he revealed it to people: Yoma 84a. In old age he drank hot water and said it restored his youth—for intercourse, Rashi: Gittin 70a. In Shabbat 111a too. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said: ‘Rabbi Yochanan’s mother told me’—this must have been before Rabbi Yochanan was born, since she died in childbirth, as above. It is difficult to understand: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani often spoke in Rabbi Yochanan’s name; how could Rabbi Yochanan have been his teacher in Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani’s old age?—‘that Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon’s wife told her’: Bava Metzia, HaPoalim, 84b. Resh Lakish married his sister, Bava Metzia, HaSokher, and after Resh Lakish’s death his young son studied with him; see his entry. Because Resh Lakish distressed him, Resh Lakish died. Rabbi Yochanan wept because Resh Lakish had died through him, lost his reason, and they prayed that he should die: there, 84a. Accordingly, it appears that Rabbi Yochanan died close to Resh Lakish’s death. Rabbi Yochanan went to a certain place and said: ‘I am the Ben Azzai here’—a great man, able to answer whatever they ask, like Ben Azzai, who said all Israel’s sages were like a garlic peel. An elder came and asked him: ‘We learned,’ and so forth. He said: ‘The Ben Azzai here has gone,’ and asked Rabbi Yannai: Jerusalem Talmud, Bikkurim 2:2. In the Jerusalem Talmud, Kol HaTzelamim, when he died all the images of kings bent down. His burial is in Tiberias; see above, Rav Kahana. His soul was reincarnated in Rabbenu Tam; see part 1, year 4865.

(5) Tosafot, Zevachim 32b, beginning: since Ketubbot 8 answers ‘Rav is a tanna and may disagree,’ but does not answer this for Rabbi Yochanan, Rabbi Yochanan was not a tanna; see below, the rules of decision. Tosafot, Ketubbot 8a, end, likewise says Rabbi Yochanan was an amora, and did not regard Rav as a tanna, since he disagrees with him. Yet there is also a Rabbi Yochanan who was a tanna, in Nazir 65a: ‘What is the measure of the surrounding soil? Rabbi Yochanan explained,’ and so forth. See Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and below, section 9. Bava Batra 28a: Rabbi Yochanan said, ‘I heard from those going to Usha.’ Rashi explains the Sanhedrin’s ten exiles: from Yavneh to Usha, and from Usha, and so forth. There on page b: who were ‘those going to Usha’ in whose name Rabbi Yochanan spoke? Rabbi Yishmael. See Rabban Gamliel the Elder: the Sanhedrin’s exile to Usha was in Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh’s days. Rabbi Yishmael was Rabbi Meir’s teacher, Rabbi Meir was Rabbi’s teacher, and Rabbi was Rabbi Yochanan’s teacher. Thus Rabbi Yochanan, who heard Rabbi Yishmael, was presumably already grown, and so was old in Rabbi’s days. The difficulty has become too great for me to bear. Yoma 82b relates that Rabbi Yochanan’s mother smelled food on the Day of Atonement. They came before Rabbi, who said: ‘Whisper to her that it is the Day of Atonement.’ They whispered, and the child immediately became quiet. They applied to him ‘Before I formed you in the womb,’ and Rabbi Yochanan was born. It says there that another woman smelled food on the Day of Atonement. They asked Rabbi Chanina, and whispered to her, but he did not become quiet. He applied to him ‘The wicked are estranged from the womb,’ and Shabbetai the hoarder of produce was born; see his entry. Thus it appears Rabbi Yochanan was born in Rabbi’s days. It seems to me that this too compels Tosafot’s statement in Nazir above: there was a Rabbi Yochanan who was a tanna, and this tanna heard Rabbi Yishmael. ‘Rabbi Yochanan Melachshekha’: HaDar, 74a. In Kol Gaggot, 91a, the same matter appears, but without the word Melachshekha, only Rabbi Yochanan. Perhaps it is the aforementioned Rabbi Yochanan, so called because they whispered to his mother on the Day of Atonement. Tosafot there says Rashi does not read ‘Who whispered to you?’ Rabbi Yitzchak says it occurs in Torat Kohanim in several places, and so forth. In Sifrei, Reeh, Rabbi Eliezer be-Rabbi Yose HaGelili says: ‘Who whispered to you? The Torah said,’ and so forth, several times in Blessing and Curse. Some read Melachshekha as one word and explain that he was born through a whisper. End quotation. Perhaps they mean that they whispered to his mother on the Day of Atonement.

(6) Sheerit Yosef 35a, end, writes: Rabbi Yochanan lived long, as Sefer HaTerumot says, nearly 258 years, until after Rav Ashi. End quotation. I found written on a very ancient sheet that he lived four hundred years. Shalshelet HaKabbalah writes that Rabbi Yochanan lived more than three hundred years—or four hundred; see part 1, 3990—as appears in the final chapter of Yoma. [It is not found there, nor does it appear from anything there.] If so, he lived even after Rav Ashi. His intention is: since Rabbi Yochanan was born in Rabbi’s days, as above, and lived so long, he lived after Rav Ashi. ‘We possess a tradition that he died before Rav Ashi. Perhaps it was another Rabbi Yochanan, and perhaps Rabbi Yochanan ben Bag Bag’ (Shalshelet HaKabbalah 33a). Why does ‘We possess a tradition that he died before Rav Ashi’ require a tradition? Moed Katan 25b relates: when Rabbi Yochanan died—in Ein Yaakov, Rabbi Pedat—Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar began his eulogy: ‘Today is as hard for Israel as the sun’s setting at midday,’ and so forth. Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi observed seven and thirty days for him; see above, Rabbi Yochanan. How many generations were there between Rabbi Ammi and Rabbi Assi and Rav Ashi! See part 1, where he died in 4070; see there, 3990.

(7) (a) When Rav and Rabbi Yochanan disagree, the law follows Rabbi Yochanan: Tosafot, Berakhot 39b and 40b; Shabbat 53a; Megillah 5a; Bava Metzia, at the printed locator פ״ב יא׳; Bava Kamma 104b; Bekhorot 21b. Except for three: Beitzah 4b and the printed locator ה׳ יב׳. Responsa Chavvot Yair writes that this is surprising, for Chullin 95b has Rabbi Yochanan writing to Rav, ‘To our teacher’; see above, Abba Arikha. Moreover, Rav was a tanna; see his entry and above. This is not said of Rabbi Yochanan, as Tosafot, Yevamot 7b and Niddah 23b, write; see above. So too the commentator on Tamid. See Sheerit Yosef 38b, rule 8. See Responsa Darkhei Noam, Even HaEzer, section 19, 86, end of column 3: although Rabbi Yochanan’s view does not agree with Rabbi, Rabbi Yochanan was a man of great stature and a tanna, able to disagree with Rabbi. Tosafot, Ketubbot 8, write that from its not saying ‘Rabbi Yochanan is a tanna and may disagree,’ one can prove that Rabbi Yochanan was an amora; see there. One may answer that the Jerusalem Talmud regards Rabbi Yochanan as a tanna who may disagree with Rabbi, since he was a later tanna. (b) Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan: the law follows Rabbi Yochanan. There in Beitzah; Tosafot, Bava Kamma 104b and Challon 79b; see Mi SheHotziuhu 47. Tosafot, HaDar 62b: everywhere our ruling follows Rabbi Yochanan against Shmuel, but here it follows Shmuel; see there and 66a, and Tosafot, Bekhorot 21b. Responsa Chavvot Yair writes that this too is astonishing, for he too was greater than Rabbi Yochanan: Chullin 95b and 137b; Responsa Rashba, section 101. But when Rav and Shmuel disagree with Rabbi Yochanan, the law follows Rav and Shmuel. Beer Sheva, beginning of Horayot, writes that Rif regularly rules so, because Rabbi Yochanan is one against two. So too the Rosh, Chavit. See Gid HaNasheh 97, which appears to show the law follows Rabbi Yochanan (Techillat Chokhmah 54a). Tosafot, Rosh Hashanah 34b, says that although Rav and Shmuel disagree with him, our ruling follows Rabbi Yochanan against Rav and Shmuel. So too Tosafot, Chavit, 145a. (c) Rabbi Yochanan and Chizkiyah: the law follows Chizkiyah. (d) Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yannai: the law follows Rabbi Yannai; see his entry. (e) Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: the law follows Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, except that in a few places it follows Rabbi Yochanan; see his entry. (f) Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Chanina: at the end of Metziat HaIshah, Rif, Maimonides, and Beit Yosef write that the law follows Rabbi Yochanan, while Rosh and Rashba rule according to Rabbi Chanina. See Responsa Darkhei Noam, Even HaEzer, sections 15, 18, 19. (g) Rav Huna and Rabbi Yochanan: the law follows Rabbi Yochanan, Chagigah 3b, because of, and so forth. See Tosafot, Berakhot 39b, 40b, 59b. Rosh, Keitzad Mevarkhin: the law follows Rabbi Yochanan against Rav Huna, for Rav Huna has no standing against Rav, his teacher, all the more against Rabbi Yochanan. Tosafot, Menachot 32b: even against Rav, who was Rav Huna’s teacher, the law follows Rabbi Yochanan, as said in Eruvin. Rav Huna’s students did not agree with him, for they wished to place a Torah scroll on his bed in the final chapter of Moed Katan. End quotation. See Megalchin, where they write: ‘It appears that this applies even if the Torah scroll is set high, since they did not place it higher than he; so we explained in HaKometz Rabbah, where I treated it at length.’ End quotation. Beer Sheva writes: on the contrary, there they wrote the reverse. On page 103, column 4, he writes that the Tosafot of Megalchin are not the Tosafot of HaKometz Rabbah, which are the words of Rabbi Yitzchak, the Tosafot master, but rather the words of later authorities. End quotation. (h) Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yochanan: the law follows Rabbi Yochanan (Halikhot Olam and Sefer Keritot 99), because he was Rabbi Elazar’s teacher. See Bava Batra 135b and 154b; Temurah 25b. Responsa Chavvot Yair writes: Maimonides rules, Laws of the Day of Atonement Service, chapter 3, that the high priest counts lest he forget, and so forth; consequently, after the fact, it is valid if he did not count. This follows Rabbi Elazar rather than Rabbi Yochanan, Yoma 55a, because Torat Kohanim states anonymously Rabbi Elazar’s view. (i) Resh Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan: the law follows Rabbi Yochanan except for three, beginning of HaCholetz 36a and Bava Batra 129; see Chullin 77 and Tosafot 29b, and Resh Lakish’s entry. Rabbi Yochanan was Resh Lakish’s teacher: HaPoalim. So Sefer Keritot, Yemot Olam, gate 3, section 21. In Chullin, at the printed locator קל״ט ית׳, and the end of Meilah, chapter 1, Rabbi Yochanan calls Resh Lakish ‘young one.’ Although Resh Lakish uprooted mountains with his sharpness, as in Bava Metzia above—see his entry—even Rav Kahana, Rav’s student, was more outstanding in sharpness than Rabbi Yochanan; see his entry. The matter does not depend on sharpness. See Migdal Oz, Laws of Shabbat 17:13: specifically when they disagree on their own authority. So too Tosafot, Bava Metzia, HaZahav, 48. (j) Rabbi Yose bar Chanina and Rabbi Yochanan: the law follows Rabbi Yochanan. This means Rabbi Yose bar Chanina, his student; but if it is another who was older than he, the law follows Rabbi Yose bar Chanina. See his entry at great length. (k) ‘Rabbi Yochanan wondered at it’: since he wondered at it and feared to disagree, our ruling here follows Resh Lakish, who spoke in Bar Kappara’s name. Rashbam, Bava Batra 39b. It is astonishing: why need the reason that he wondered and feared to disagree, and therefore the law follows Bar Kappara? Even had he explicitly disagreed, one should rule according to Bar Kappara, who was Rabbi Yochanan’s teacher. See below, HaGozel Batra, 112b: ‘Rabbi Yochanan wondered at it.’

(8) These were Rabbi Yochanan’s teachers. (a) Rabbenu HaKadosh: Pesachim 3b and Ellu Terefot, for Rav served before Rabbi sitting, and Rabbi Yochanan standing; see his entry. Menachot 88b: ‘Rabbi Yochanan said: Rabbi said.’ Zevachim 99b: another version, ‘Rabbi Yonatan said: Rabbi said’—new Talmud edition. Sotah 36b: in Rabbi’s name. (b) Rabbi Yannai: HaIshah Rabbah 92b, Rabbi Yannai said, and so forth. Rabbi Yochanan told him: ‘Master, is this not our Mishnah?’ and so forth. He replied: ‘Had I not lifted the shard for you,’ and so forth. Resh Lakish told Rabbi Yochanan: ‘Had not a great man praised you,’ and so forth. He asked Rabbi Yannai: Rosh Hashanah 15a. Rabbi Yannai told him: ‘What is the difference between me and you?’ Rashi explains: that I know how to explain the Mishnah better than you, Tolin 140a. Responsa Chavvot Yair, section 152, says Rabbi Yannai told Rabbi Yochanan that he had thus received from his teachers, but in understanding and intellectual examination there was no difference. Alternatively, Rabbi Yochanan received his recompense, for he himself said this to Isi bar Hini; see his entry. Mi SheMet 154b: ‘If Rabbi Yochanan denies Rabbi Elazar, his student, he will not deny Rabbi Yannai, his teacher.’ Rashi, Reshit HaGez 137b, end: Rabbi Yannai was Rabbi Yochanan’s teacher. Jerusalem Talmud, Kiddushin 1:4: Rabbi Yochanan was Rabbi Yannai’s student. Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot, mishnah 1: Rabbi Yochanan asked Rabbi Yannai, before Rabbi Shmuel ben Yehotzadak’s bier—I think it should read Shimon—‘He consecrated his burnt offering.’ Rashbam, HaSefinah 84b, and Ein Maamidin; see Rabbi Yannai’s entry at length. (c) Rabbi Oshaya Rabbah: Bene HaIr—I did not find it there—he learned before him eleven years. Under aleph, Rabbi Oshaya Rabbah, Yuchasin writes: ‘Keitzad Meabbarin and Bene HaIr: Rabbi Oshaya was Rabbi Yochanan’s teacher for eighteen years.’ End quotation. Jerusalem Talmud, beginning of Keitzad Meabbarin and HaNechenakin, halakhah 6: for thirteen years Rabbi Yochanan regularly came before his teacher Rabbi Oshaya, even without a need to learn, solely to honor him. Babylonian Talmud, beginning of Keitzad Meabbarin, 53a: Rabbi Yochanan said, ‘I grew up with Rabbi Oshaya Berabbi for eighteen days and learned only one thing.’ He had twelve students. In eighteen days Rabbi Yochanan learned each one’s heart and wisdom. They sat four to a cubit. Jerusalem Talmud, Terumot 10:3: Rabbi Yochanan said, ‘When we used to go to Rabbi Hoshaya Rabbah at Caesarea to learn Torah.’ Yevamot, HaBa Al Yevimto 57a: Rabbi Yochanan asked Rabbi Oshaya, who remained silent and told him nothing. Resh Lakish asked him, and he resolved it for him. Rabbi Yehudah Nesia told Rabbi Oshaya: ‘Is Rabbi Yochanan not a great man?’ (d) Chizkiyah son of Rabbi Chiyya: Ellu Kesharim 112b and Passin 24a; concerning him Chizkiyah said: ‘This is no ordinary human.’ Tosafot, Sukkah 44a, the comment beginning ‘VeHaAmar,’ and Tosafot, Menachot 23b, end. See Menachot 78b, Zevachim 56b, Chagigah 9a, and Mi SheHotziuhu 50a, where Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan dispute. Kiddushin 51a, Rashi explains that Chizkiyah was Rabbi Yochanan’s teacher. Rabbi Chiyya’s sons and Rabbi Yochanan dispute: Yoma 5b. Tosafot, HaMegareish 84b: Chizkiyah was his teacher. (e) He also received from Rabbi Benaah. (f) Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak was his teacher, in Sanhedrin. In Rabbi Shimon B.Y.’s name: Yoma 22b, two things; Pesachim 95b; Avodah Zarah 59a, beginning; Taanit 28b; HaYashen 27a; Bava Metzia 27a. ‘In Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai’s name’ should read ‘Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak.’ See Tosafot, Niddah 10b: ‘Rabbi Yochanan said in Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak’s name’ implies that he was his teacher. In Zeh Borer 26a, Resh Lakish calls Rabbi Shimon B.Y. a cattle herder, and Rabbi Yochanan did not protest for his teacher’s honor. Rabbenu Tam says there were two. End quotation. See his entry at length. (g) Rosh, Mi SheMet, writes that Bar Kappara was his teacher; so too Rif, and Rosh, Avodah Zarah, chapter 2: Chizkiyah and Bar Kappara were Rabbi Yochanan’s teachers. (h) Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi too was his teacher; see his entry, where some say Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was his student. (i) Rabbi Yose ben Nehorai was his teacher; see his entry. (j) Sefer Keritot writes: Rav, Shmuel, and Rabbi Yochanan received from Rabbi Chiyya in 530 of the contracts era. End quotation. It requires examination whether Rabbi Yochanan received from Rabbi Chiyya.

(9) I shall now set before you those in whose names Rabbi Yochanan spoke; by the principles I have written, judge and infer whether they were his teachers. Rabbi Yochanan said: ‘Abba bar Abba told me’: Jerusalem Talmud, Tamid Nishchat. In Rabbi Abba bar Mammal’s name, so writes Yuchasin—I did not find it; see his entry. ‘Rabbi Ittai taught us.’ In Rabbi Eliezer be-Rabbi Yose HaGelili’s name: Vayikra Rabbah, sections 18 and 19 and beginning of Acharei. In Rabbi Eliezer’s name—see his entry—and he was Rabbi Yochanan’s student. In Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Shimon’s name. In Rabbi Elazar de-Roma’s name. In Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov’s name: Berakhot 40b and Sotah 43b, several things. Rabbi Yochanan said: ‘I have a received tradition from Rabbi Elazar be-Rabbi Tzadok’: Jerusalem Talmud, Avodah Zarah 2:9. In Rabbi Benai’s name. Rabbi Yochanan said: ‘Rabbi Binyamin bar Levi said.’ Rabbi Yochanan said: ‘Bardela taught.’ He questioned Rabban Gamliel Berabbi. He questioned Rabbi Gamliel Zuga. Rabbi Yochanan said: ‘Zavdi ben Levi taught.’ Rabbi Yochanan said: ‘Rabbi Chiyya said’: Bava Metzia 40a. Zevachim 25b has ‘Rabbi Chiyya said: Rabbi Yochanan said.’ It appears that it should read ‘R. Chiyya bar Abba said: Rabbi Yochanan said’ [digital witness אר״ת, probably for אר״ח; conjectural reading]. So too is implied there: Rabbi Zeira told Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, and so forth; and ‘Rabbi Yochanan said: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said.’ See above, Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba. Rabbi Yochanan said: ‘Thus said Rabbi Chalafta of Hina.’ He called Rabbi Chanina bar Sisi ‘Rabbi.’ Rav Chanina transmitted in his name. ‘Rabbi Chanina said’: Kirah 47a. He learned aggadah from Rabbi Chananyah. In Rabbi Yehudah bar Ilai’s name: Keitzad Mevarkhin 35b, two things; Arvei Pesachim 114a; Yoma 10a; Gittin 81a. In Rabbi’s name: ‘This teaches that his bow returned to its strength,’ Sotah 36b; Menachot 88b, ‘Rabbi said.’ He spoke before Rabbi Yehudah Nesia; see his entry. In Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira’s name. He asked Rabbi Yehudah bar Levi. In Rabbi Yehudah be-Rabbi Shimon’s name; see his entry. In Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi’s name. Some report it in Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananyah’s name: Keitzad Tzolin 79a and Menachot 26a. In Rabbi Yonatan’s name. In Rabbi Yose ben Zimra’s name. In Rabbi Yose HaGelili’s name. In Rabbi Yose ben Kisma’s name. In Rabbi Yose’s name: Shabbat 118a and Berakhot 7a, many things, and Bereshit Rabbah, section 4. In Rabbi Yose ben Katzarta’s name. In Rabbi Yose ben Yehoshua’s name. In Abba Yose ben Abba’s name. ‘Rabbi Yose bar Chanina said’; see his entry. Rabbi Yochanan said: ‘Yosef of Hutzal asked.’ In Rabbi Yishmael’s name: Chagigah 9a; Yoma 3b; Yevamot 45a, 68b, end, 74a, end; Kiddushin 75b. In Bereshit Rabbah 45 this is in Rabbi Shimon’s name. Sotah 16a and 26b; Avodah Zarah 11; see above what I wrote. In Rabbi Meir’s name: Megillah 27a; Kiddushin 57b; Sotah 35a, 36b, 42b, 46b; Temurah 3a; Avodah Zarah 24b. In Rabbi Menachem of Yodfat’s name. In Menachem of Galya’s name. In Rabbi Nechunyah of the Valley of Beit Chortan’s name. Nicha bar Sava. Rabbi Yochanan in Zeira’s name. In Rabbi Akiva’s name: Devarim Rabbah, chapter 2. In Rabbi Pinchas ben Aruva’s name. He asked Shmuel. In Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai’s name: Berakhot 7b, many things, and 10a, 31a, 46a, 55a, end; Kol Kitvei 118b; HaDar 64b; Pesachim 87b; Yoma 5b; Sukkah 29b, 30a, and 45; Megillah 6b and Bene HaIr; Beitzah 16a; Yevamot 23a, 45, 93a, 103a; Ketubbot 52b, 67b; Kiddushin 57a, 68b; Nedarim 64b; Sotah 4b, 12b; Bava Kamma 17; Bava Metzia 27a—this is a scribal error and should read ‘in Rabbi Shimon ben Yehotzadak’s name’—and 58; Bava Batra 109, 116; Sanhedrin 24, 39, 46, 70, 93, 103; Horayot; Makkot 14; Shevuot 18, 21; Menachot 99; Arakhin 17; Bekhorot 31b; Keritot 27; Niddah 21, 61; Bereshit Rabbah, section 7; Bamidbar Rabbah, chapter 4; Eichah Rabbah. He heard Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar teach; this requires examination. In Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel’s name: Megillah 27a. In Rabbi Shimon HaMechozi’s name. Rabbi Yochanan said in Ben Azzai’s name, at the end of Nazir, 65a, end. These are its words: ‘He says as this tanna, for it was taught: What is the measure of the surrounding soil? Rabbi Yochanan said in Ben Azzai’s name: He takes earth,’ and so forth. Tosafot write: Rabbi Yochanan is not Rabbi Yochanan the amora, but Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri. Tosafot, Ketubbot 8a, end, write: at the end of Nazir there is also a Rabbi Yochanan who was a tanna. Their intention is that ‘as this tanna, for it was taught’ proves that he was a tanna of the baraita; they did not write that he was Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri. This does not seem right to me: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri was Rabbi Akiva’s colleague, and Ben Azzai was Rabbi Akiva’s student; how could he speak in his name? It seems likely to me that this is Rabbi Yochanan ben Yeshua, son of Rabbi Akiva’s father-in-law, whom we find speaking in accordance with Ben Azzai. But nowhere in the Talmud have we found Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri mentioning Ben Azzai. Rav Tachlifa of the West taught him.

(10) These are Rabbi Yochanan’s students listed by Sheerit Yosef and Yuchasin. What I marked with a semicircle is what I added; some require examination in their places. ⬤ Rabbi Abba. ⬤ Rabbi Abba bar Mammal, in his name. ⬤ Rabbi Abba bar Yasi. ⬤ Rabbi Abba bar Bizna. Rabbi Abba bar Yaakov. Rabbi Abba bar Yirmeyah—I did not find him speaking in Rabbi Yochanan’s name. Rabbi Abba of Caesarea, Yuchasin—we have not found him speaking in Rabbi Yochanan’s name. Rabbi Abba of Haifa, Yuchasin—we have not found that he was Rabbi Yochanan’s student. ⬤ Rabbi Abba bar Kahana. ⬤ Rabbi Abba son of Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba. ⬤ Rabbi Abbahu. Rabbi Avin. ⬤ Avin bar Chisda. Rabbi Adda of Caesarea. ⬤ Rav Adda bar Avuya, Yuchasin—I did not find mention of him. Rav Acha bar Chana. Rav Acha bar Avira—I did not find him speaking in Rabbi Yochanan’s name. Rav Acha bar Avya. Rav Acha bar Abba. ⬤ Rav Acha bar Yaakov. Rav Achai—I did not find him speaking in Rabbi Yochanan’s name. Ayvi bar Nagri. Rabbi Idi. Rabbi Ila. Ilfa—this requires examination; it appears he was his colleague. Rabbi Ilai. Rabbi Ilai be-Rabbi Berekhiah said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name. Rabbi Elazar. Rabbi Ammi. ⬤ Rabbi Ammi Shappir Naeh. Rabbi Assi. ⬤ Rav Ashi said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name. Rav Ashi bar Abba said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name—I did not find mention of this. ⬤ Beha. Rav Biva. Rav Bivi. Rav Bivi bar Avin. ⬤ Belavvati. Rabbi Binyamin bar Yefet. Rabbi Binyamin bar Giddel. Rabbi Bata said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name, Yuchasin—I did not find it; see Beha. ⬤ Rav Giddel. Rabbi Dostai bar Matton. Rav Dimi. Rav Huna. ⬤ Rav Huna bar Ammi said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name, Yuchasin—I did not find it; see Chana bar Ammi, who said in Rabbi Pedat’s name, in Rabbi Yochanan’s name. Huna of Sepphoris. ⬤ Rav Hoshaya, Rabbah’s brother. There is also a dispute with Rabbi Hoshaya [ורבי הושעיה פליגי]. ⬤ Rabbi Zeira. Rav Zakkai. Zakkai the butcher. Rabbi Zeira was his student and spoke in his name. Rabbi Chaviva—I did not find him. ⬤ Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin. Rabbi Chiyya in Rabbi Yochanan’s name: Jerusalem Talmud, Megillah 3:8 and HaMaddir, halakhah 7. This requires examination, for Chizkiyah son of Rabbi Chiyya was Rabbi Yochanan’s teacher. It appears it should read ‘Rav Chiyya bar Abba.’ In the Jerusalem Talmud, Ein Omdin, mishnah 1, ‘Rabbi Abba said: Rabbi Chiyya said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name.’ I think it should read ‘Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said,’ or ‘Rabbi Abba said: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said.’ We likewise find in Shabbat 113a that Rabbi Abba spoke in Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba’s name, as appears there in Rif. ⬤ Rav Chiyya be-Rav Huna. ⬤ Rav Chiyya bar Ashi. ⬤ Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba. ⬤ Rabbi Chiyya bar Yosef. Rabbi Chelbo. ⬤ Rav Chama bar Buzi—this requires examination. Rav Chana bar Shauna, Rabbi Yochanan’s student—I did not find him speaking in Rabbi Yochanan’s name. ⬤ Rav Chana bar Abba. Rav Chana of Sepphoris; see Huna of Sepphoris. Rav Chana Petorai was before him. Rabbi Yochanan went to visit Rabbi Chanina, heard that he had died, and sent for Sabbath garments and tore them: Jerusalem Talmud, Horayot 3:6; see above. Rav Chanina bar Yosef—this requires examination. ⬤ Rav Chanina, Rabbah’s brother. Rabbi Chanina Shilka transmitted in his name. Rav Chanan bar Rava. Rabbi Chananyah transmitted in his name. Rav Chisda—this requires examination. Rabbi Tavot the fowler—I did not find him speaking in Rabbi Yochanan’s name, only in Shmuel’s. Rabbi Yehudah Nesia, the second. Rabbi Yehudah bar Idi. Rabbi Yehudah Gelustera, Rabbi Yochanan’s student, Yuchasin—I did not find it; it appears to be a scribal error. Rabbi Yehoshua of Sikhnin transmitted in his name; see Rabbi Chanina Shilka. ⬤ Rabbi Yudan transmitted in his name—this requires examination. Rabbi Yochanan ben Maroya transmitted in his name. Rabbi Yonah. Rabbi Yostai bar Matton. Rabbi Yose ben Yose. ⬤ With Rabbi Yose of Malchaya. ⬤ Rabbi Yose bar Zemina transmitted in his name. Rabbi Yose of Sidon. Rabbi Yose ben Elyakim lived in his time, Yuchasin—I did not find it. Rabbi Yose bar Chanina; see his entry. Rabbi Yosef bar Abba. ⬤ Rav Yosef bar Chama. Rabbi Yaakov. Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi, a student-colleague. Rabbi Yaakov bar Acha. Rabbi Yitzchak. Rav Yitzchak bar Yosef. Rabbi Yitzchak Nappacha. With Rabbi Yitzchak Paska. Rabbi Yitzchak Kaskasaa. Rabbi Yitzchak Tavla. Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yaakov bar Giyori. ⬤ Rabbi Yitzchak of Kefar Akko. ⬤ Rabbi Yitzchak bar Mari transmitted in his name. ⬤ Rabbi Yitzchak of Kefar Itosh, Rabbi Yochanan’s student, Yuchasin—I did not find him speaking in Rabbi Yochanan’s name. Rabbi Yitzchak Migdalaah: Yuchasin writes that he lived in his time—I did not find it. Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elazar; see above. ⬤ Rabbi Chiyya be-Rabbi Chiyya Ketuvah [ר' חייא בר' חייא כתובה; name/wording unresolved]. ⬤ Rabbi Yitzchak Dehava. Rabbi Yitzchak ben Elyashuv lived in his time, Yuchasin—I did not find it. Rabbi Yirmeyah bar Abba. Rabbi Yirmeyah. Rav Kahana said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name. Rabbi Keruspedai. Rabbi Levatti, Rabbi Yochanan’s student, Yuchasin—I did not find it. Rabbi Levi transmitted in his name; see Rabbi Chanina Shilka. Rav Machsya. ⬤ Bar Idi. Rabbi Mani. Rabbi Misha. ⬤ Rabbi Mishon bar Nagdi. Rav Menashya bar Yirmeyah—I did not find it. Rav Mari. Rav Mari be-Rav Huna be-Rav Yirmeyah bar Abba—this requires examination. Rabbi Marinos transmitted in his name; see his entry. Rabbi Maron asked him. Rabbi Nachum, Rabbi Ila’s brother, asked before him. ⬤ Rav Nachman transmitted in his name. Rav Natan bar Tovyah. Rav Natan bar Oshaya. Rav Safra. Eva, Rabbi Yochanan’s student, Yuchasin—I did not find mention of this. Ulla. ⬤ Ulla bar Yishmael. ⬤ Rav Ukvan of Meishan. Rabbi Ila. ⬤ Rav Amram. Rav Anan—I did not find him. Rabbi Pedat. ⬤ Rabbi Pazi. Rabbi Parnakh. Rabbi Krispa transmitted in his name. ⬤ Rabbi Reuven transmitted in his name—this requires examination. Rava bar Chanina. ⬤ Rava said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name—this requires examination. Rabbah bar Natan. Rabbah transmitted in his name and was his student—this requires examination there. Rabbah bar bar Chana. Rabbah bar Chanina. Rabbah bar Ulla. Rabbah be-Rav Huna. ⬤ Rabbah bar Shauna, Rabbi Yochanan’s student, Yuchasin—I did not find mention of this. Ravin transmitted in his name. Resh Lakish. Rami bar Chilkiyah—I did not find mention of this. Rav Sheizvi. Rav Shmuel. ⬤ Rav Shmuel be-Rav Yitzchak. ⬤ Rav Shmuel bar Abba. ⬤ Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani, or bar Nachman; see above, and this requires examination. ⬤ Rav Shmuel bar Yehudah. Rav Shisha, son of Rav Idi. Rabbi Simlai. Rav Shemen bar Abba HaKohen. Rav Shemen—this requires examination. Rabbi Shimon bar Zerud. ⬤ Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi. Rabbi Shimon ben Yaakov of Tyre; see above. ⬤ Rabbi Shimon bar Abba. When Rav Dimi came, he said: ‘Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Shimon, Rabbi Yochanan’s students, say’: Berakhot, chapter 3, 21b. In HaOmer 66b, end, Rabbi Shimon spoke to Rabbi Yochanan. I do not know who these Rabbi Shimon and Rabbi Yehudah are. Rabbi Shimon ben Elyakim asked him. Rabbi Shefatyah. Rav Sheshet said in Rabbi Yochanan’s name. Rav Tanchum bar Marion. Rav Tanchum of Parvad taught him. Rabbi Tanchum—I did not find him.
